title: How to Put a Price on the Future
subtitle: A company is worth the cash it'll throw off for years. A bond is a stream of future payments. So how do you price a river of money that hasn't arrived yet?
hook: Almost everything valuable is really a *promise of future money*: a rental spits out rent, a bond pays coupons, a company earns profits for decades. So the trillion-dollar question is: what is a stream of *future* cash worth **today**? Yesterday you learned to run compounding backwards. Today we turn that one move into the master tool of finance — **discounted cash flow** — the thing every analyst, investor, and founder secretly runs in their head.

builds_on.label: The Most Important Curve in Finance

sections.heading: One future payment → today's value
sections.body:
Recall discounting: `Present = Future / (1 + r)ⁿ`. At a 10% discount rate, $110 next year is worth $100 now; $121 in two years is *also* worth $100 now. The further away the cash, the more you shrink it — because waiting costs you (opportunity, risk, inflation).

The discount rate `r` is the dial. Crank it up (riskier, or higher interest rates) and future money is worth *less* today. That single dial is why rising interest rates hammer the price of everything from tech stocks to houses.

sections.heading: Many payments → discounted cash flow (DCF)
sections.body:
A real asset pays out over *many* years. So you **discount each future payment back to today and add them up**. That sum is the asset's fair value right now. That's the whole DCF method:

`Value = CF₁/(1+r) + CF₂/(1+r)² + CF₃/(1+r)³ + …`

Estimate the future cash flows, pick a discount rate for the risk, discount, sum. Every valuation you'll ever see — a stock, a startup, a rental, a bond — is a dressed-up version of this.

sections.caption: Each future year's cash gets shrunk back to 'today dollars' — more shrinkage the further out — then summed into one value.

sections.label: Garbage in, garbage out
sections.body: DCF feels precise, but it's only as good as two guesses: the **future cash flows** and the **discount rate**. Nudge the discount rate a little and the 'value' swings wildly — which is exactly how two smart analysts value the same company at half and double. Use DCF to understand *what drives* value, not to pretend you've found one true number.

takeaways: Most assets are a **stream of future cash** — the job is pricing it today.
Discount each future payment: `PV = Future / (1+r)ⁿ`; farther out = shrunk more.
**DCF** = discount every future cash flow and **sum** them into one value.
The **discount rate** is the master dial — higher rates crush the value of future money.
DCF is only as good as its inputs; use it to see *what drives* value, not for false precision.

quiz.q: At a 10% rate, is $121 received in 2 years worth more or less than $100 today?
quiz.explain: $121 / 1.1² = $100. Discounting future cash back is the heart of DCF.

quiz.q: Interest rates rise sharply. What happens to the present value of far-off future cash?
options: It falls — a higher discount rate shrinks future money more
quiz.explain: Higher r means bigger denominators — future cash is worth less today. This is why rate hikes hit long-duration assets hardest.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: Yesterday's compounding vs. today's DCF — what's the relationship?
options: DCF is compounding run in reverse: instead of growing money forward, you shrink future money back to today
They only both use the letter r
quiz.explain: Compounding multiplies forward by (1+r); discounting divides backward by (1+r). DCF just does that for many payments and adds them.

tg_quiz.q: Rates jump. The present value of far-future cash…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — a higher discount rate shrinks future money.
tg_quiz.wrong: It falls — bigger r means future cash is worth less today.
tg_quiz.explain: Why rate hikes hit long-duration assets (like tech stocks) hardest.
